topic_and_scope: This document examines the skeletal muscle–adipose tissue axis (AMA) and the proposed Adipo–Muscle Ratio (AMR) as a framework to redefine obesity, assess cardiometabolic risk, and guide treatment, with emphasis on preserving skeletal muscle during weight loss and integrating novel pharmacotherapies.
main_themes: AMA/AMR as a new framework for obesity definition, risk stratification, and management beyond BMI
Preservation and enhancement of skeletal muscle mass and function during weight loss to maintain metabolic health
Translational pathway from myokine/adipokine biology to diagnostics, biomarkers, and combination pharmacotherapies
main_findings: Skeletal muscle mass and function are central determinants of insulin sensitivity and metabolic health; insulin resistance in skeletal muscle can precede beta-cell dysfunction and is, in principle, reversible with targeted interventions.

Relying on BMI as the primary obesity metric is limited; adopting AMA/AMR could better reflect cardiometabolic risk and guide treatment, but requires development of non-invasive, accurate AMR measurements and international consensus.

key_gaps.description: No universal consensus on diagnostic criteria for sarcopenic obesity (SO); standard definitions and measurement approaches are lacking.

AMR as a clinical biomarker requires validation across diverse populations and settings, including demonstration of added predictive value beyond BMI and existing measures; this translation is currently implied rather than established.

future_directions.title: Establish international consensus defining obesity via AMA/AMR rather than BMI
future_directions.rationale: The article argues that BMI is a blunt, insufficient metric for obesity and cardiometabolic risk. A global panel should harmonize definitions and thresholds for AMR, incorporating age, sex, and ethnicity. The next steps include drafting consensus guidelines, benchmarking AMR against morbidity and mortality in multiple cohorts, and disseminating recommendations to update clinical practice guidelines within 5–8 years.

future_directions.title: Develop and validate point-of-care AMR assessment tools
future_directions.rationale: AMR requires non-invasive, accurate measurement of SM and AT mass at or near the point of care. Research should translate imaging-based measures (DXA/MRI) into portable, bedside tools (e.g., advanced bioelectrical impedance analyses) with standardized protocols. Validation against gold-standard imaging in diverse populations is essential, followed by integration into routine clinical workflows.

future_directions.title: Create large multi-ethnic prospective cohorts to characterize AMA components
future_directions.rationale: Ethnic-specific variance in obesity risk and AMR needs thorough mapping. Prospective cohorts should collect comprehensive body composition data (SM/AT/IMCL), metabolic biomarkers, and outcomes (T2D, CVD, mortality). Analyses should identify AMR thresholds that predict risk across populations and adjust for socio-economic confounders, informing tailored interventions.

future_directions.title: Trial GLP-1-based therapies co-administered with SM-preserving agents to minimize SM loss during weight reduction
future_directions.rationale: GLP-1–driven weight loss can entail significant loss of SM. A randomized trial combining GLP-1–based therapy with a SM-preserving agent (e.g., a myostatin/ActRII pathway modulator like bimagrumab) should evaluate effects on AMR, insulin sensitivity, gait speed, and quality of life. Subgroups (older adults, individuals with T2D) and long-term safety outcomes should be included to inform clinical guidelines.

future_directions.title: Advance peripheral SM-preserving pharmacotherapies and assess long-term safety
future_directions.rationale: Myostatin/Activin A pathway inhibitors show promise for preserving lean mass during NEB, and combination strategies with GLP-1 therapies may enhance metabolic outcomes. Systematic preclinical-to-clinical development with phased trials should monitor efficacy on AMR and functional endpoints, as well as safety signals (e.g., off-target effects, metabolic complications) over extended follow-up.

future_directions.title: Investigate Apelin receptor agonists and spexin as SM-mass–preserving therapies
future_directions.rationale: Apelin and spexin pathways have shown potential to improve SM mass and metabolic function in preclinical models. Early-phase human trials should determine dosing, safety, and impact on AMR and insulin sensitivity, guiding subsequent larger efficacy studies and potential combinatorial regimens.

future_directions.title: Evaluate peripheral CB1R antagonists for AMR improvement with favorable safety profiles
future_directions.rationale: Peripheral CB1R modulation (e.g., INV-202) has demonstrated weight loss and metabolic benefits in early trials, with potential to improve body composition. Focused safety assessments and efficacy trials should quantify effects on AMR, SM mass, hepatic/renal function, and long-term metabolic outcomes, avoiding CNS-related adverse effects.

future_directions.title: Define optimized nutritional strategies that preserve SM during NEB, emphasizing leucine-rich protein with resistance training
future_directions.rationale: Evidence supports high-protein intake and leucine-rich foods to mitigate SM loss during NEB, especially when paired with resistance exercise. Randomized trials should specify protein type (animal vs. plant), leucine targets (7–12 g/day), timing relative to exercise, and compliance, with primary endpoints including AMR changes, SM mass, and insulin sensitivity.

future_directions.title: Develop and validate serum/urine myokine–adipokine panels as non-invasive AMR biomarkers
future_directions.rationale: A biomarker signature could enable non-invasive, rapid estimation of SM and AT mass and the AMR at the point of care. Research should identify robust myokine/adipokine panels, validate against imaging measures, standardize assays, and assess predictive value for cardiometabolic outcomes to support clinical decision-making and monitoring.
